description: Series and parallel circuit rules, mains AC vs battery DC, plug wiring, electrical power, and the National Grid.
content_html:
Series and Parallel Circuits

In a series circuit, all components are in a single continuous loop. This means:

• Current is the same at every point in the circuit — charge is not used up.
• Potential difference is shared between components — the sum of individual voltages equals the supply voltage.
• Total resistance = sum of individual resistances: \(R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\)
• If one component fails, the circuit breaks and all components stop working.

In a parallel circuit, components are on separate branches. This means:

• Potential difference is the same across each branch (and equals the supply voltage).
• Current splits between branches — more current flows through the branch with lower resistance.
• Total resistance is lower than the smallest individual resistance because there are more paths for current.
• If one component fails, the others continue to work. This is why household appliances use parallel wiring.

Key Fact

Series: current the same everywhere; PD shared. Parallel: PD the same across each branch; current shared. Adding resistors in parallel decreases total resistance (more paths available).

Series: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 4 Ω in series: \(R_{\text{total}} = 6 + 4 = 10 \text{ } \Omega\). If the supply is 20 V, the current everywhere is \(I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{20}{10} = 2 \text{ A}\). The 6 Ω resistor has \(V = 2 \times 6 = 12 \text{ V}\) across it; the 4 Ω resistor has \(V = 2 \times 4 = 8 \text{ V}\). Sum: \(12 + 8 = 20 \text{ V}\) ✓

Parallel: Two 6 Ω resistors in parallel. Each has 12 V across it. Current in each branch: \(I = \frac{12}{6} = 2 \text{ A}\). Total current from supply: \(2 + 2 = 4 \text{ A}\). Effective total resistance: \(R = \frac{12}{4} = 3 \text{ } \Omega\) — lower than either individual resistor.

AC and DC

Direct current (DC) flows in one direction only — this is what batteries and solar cells produce. Alternating current (AC) constantly reverses direction. The UK mains supply is AC at a frequency of 50 Hz (50 complete cycles per second) and a voltage of about 230 V. On an oscilloscope trace, AC appears as a sine wave oscillating above and below zero; DC appears as a flat horizontal line.

Key Fact

UK domestic mains: AC at 230 V and 50 Hz. Batteries: DC. AC can have its voltage changed by a transformer; DC cannot. On an oscilloscope trace: AC = wave, DC = flat line.

Mains Wiring and Safety

A UK three-pin plug contains three wires, each with a specific colour and function:

• Live (brown) — carries the AC supply at about 230 V. Always dangerous, even when the appliance is switched off, because it remains connected to the mains supply.
• Neutral (blue) — completes the circuit at approximately 0 V. Current flows in through the live and out through the neutral.
• Earth (green and yellow striped) — a safety wire connected to the metal casing of an appliance. Provides a low-resistance path to earth if a fault causes the casing to become live.

A fuse is always in the live wire. If the current exceeds the fuse rating, the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit, preventing overheating or fire. The earth wire and fuse work together: if the live wire accidentally touches the metal casing, a surge of current flows through the earth wire, blowing the fuse and cutting the supply. A residual current device (RCD) provides faster protection by detecting any imbalance between live and neutral currents and cutting the circuit within milliseconds.

Appliances with plastic casings (such as hairdryers and power drills) use double insulation. The plastic casing cannot become live because it is an insulator, so there is no risk of the user receiving an electric shock even if the wiring inside develops a fault. These appliances are marked with a double-square symbol and do not require an earth wire. This makes them safe in damp environments where a metal-cased appliance with a faulty earth could be particularly dangerous.

Electrical Power and Energy

Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer. The key equations are:

$$P = V \times I \qquad P = I^2 \times R$$

Where \(P\) is power (W), \(V\) is potential difference (V), \(I\) is current (A), and \(R\) is resistance (Ω). The second equation is useful when voltage is not known. The total energy transferred is:

$$E = P \times t$$

Where \(E\) is energy (J) and \(t\) is time (s). For domestic billing, energy is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh): one kWh = a 1 kW appliance running for 1 hour. Cost = energy (kWh) × price per kWh.

Key Fact

Power equations: \(P = VI\), \(P = I^2R\). Energy transferred: \(E = Pt\). Domestic energy unit: kilowatt-hour (kWh). Cost (pence) = energy (kWh) × price per unit.

The National Grid

The National Grid transmits electricity from power stations to consumers across the UK. Electricity is transmitted at very high voltages (up to several hundred thousand volts) and correspondingly low currents to minimise energy losses in the cables. Since the power wasted as heat in cables is \(P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 R\), a smaller current dramatically reduces losses — squaring the current means even a small reduction in current makes a large difference.

Step-up transformers at power stations increase voltage (and reduce current) for long-distance transmission. Step-down transformers at local substations reduce the voltage to 230 V for safe household use. Transformers only work with AC because they rely on a changing magnetic field in the core to induce a voltage in the secondary coil; a DC supply would produce a constant field and no induced voltage.
exam_tip_html: For circuit questions, always identify whether the circuit is series or parallel before applying any rules. A common error is assuming that adding more components always increases resistance — this is only true in series; in parallel, adding more branches decreases total resistance. For plug wiring questions, learn the colour codes: live = brown, neutral = blue, earth = green/yellow. For National Grid questions, always explain that high voltage means low current, and link this to \(P = I^2R\) to show why lower current reduces heat losses.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Series circuits: current the same throughout; PD shared; total resistance = sum of individual resistances. Parallel circuits: PD the same across each branch; current shared; total resistance is less than any individual branch.
  • UK mains supply: AC at 230 V, 50 Hz. Plug: live (brown) at 230 V, neutral (blue) at 0 V, earth (green/yellow) for safety. Fuse always in the live wire. Power: \(P = VI\) or \(P = I^2R\).
  • The National Grid transmits at high voltage / low current to minimise heat losses (\(P = I^2R\)). Step-up transformers increase voltage for transmission; step-down transformers reduce it for domestic use. Transformers only work with AC.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is true about components connected in parallel?
A) They share the same current
B) They share the same potential difference
C) The total resistance increases as more components are added
D) The circuit stops working if one component fails
practice_questions.marks:
B) They share the same potential difference [1 mark]
In a parallel circuit, each branch has the same PD (the supply voltage). Current is shared between branches. Adding components in parallel decreases total resistance. A single branch failing does not stop others.

practice_questions.text: State the UK mains supply voltage and frequency.
practice_questions.marks:
230 V and 50 Hz [1 mark]
(Both values required for the mark)

practice_questions.text:
A kettle has a power rating of 2 200 W. It is connected to the 230 V mains supply.
Calculate the current drawn by the kettle. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
practice_questions.marks:
Identify equation: P = VI, so I = P ÷ V [1 mark]
Substitute: I = 2200 ÷ 230 [1 mark]
I = 9.565… ≈ 9.6 A (2 s.f.) [1 mark]
Unit: A (amperes) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain why electricity is transmitted through the National Grid at high voltage and low current, rather than at low voltage and high current. Refer to a relevant equation in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that cables have resistance. Uses \(P = I^2R\) to show that power wasted as heat depends on current squared — so a smaller current dramatically reduces power losses. High voltage achieves the same power transfer at lower current (\(P = VI\)). [3 marks]
Secure: States high voltage gives low current and mentions reduced energy losses, but does not reference the equation. [2 marks]
Developing: States 'high voltage is more efficient' without further explanation. [1 mark]
Emerging: Vague or incorrect. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the earth wire and the fuse in a three-pin plug as a combined safety system. Include what happens if the live wire contacts the metal casing of an appliance.
practice_questions.marks: If the live wire contacts the metal casing, a large current surges through the earth wire to ground [1 mark]. This large current exceeds the fuse rating, causing the fuse wire to melt and break the live wire connection, cutting off the supply and preventing electrocution or fire [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
A student uses a 60 W laptop for 3 hours per day for 30 days. Electricity costs 28p per kWh.
Calculate the total cost of running the laptop over 30 days. Show all steps.
practice_questions.marks:
Power in kW: 60 W = 0.06 kW [1 mark]
Time: 3 h/day × 30 days = 90 h [1 mark]
Energy = 0.06 × 90 = 5.4 kWh [2 marks: 1 for method, 1 for value]
Cost = 5.4 × 28 = 151.2p = £1.51 [2 marks: 1 for method, 1 for correct answer with unit]

Mastering: All steps shown, correct answer in pence or pounds.
Secure: Correct method; minor arithmetic error.
Developing: Converts W to kW or calculates energy but not cost.
Emerging: Uses kW and hours but does not complete the calculation.

knowledge_checks.q: In a series circuit with three resistors of 2 Ω, 4 Ω and 6 Ω, what is the total resistance?
What colour is the live wire in a UK three-pin plug?
In a parallel circuit, the potential difference across each branch is _____ as the supply voltage.
The National Grid transmits electricity at high voltage and low _____ to reduce heat losses in the cables.
Match each wire in a UK plug to its function:
right: Carries the AC supply at 230 V
Safety wire — low-resistance path to earth if fault occurs

flashcard_questions.q: In a series circuit, how does current vary at different points?
flashcard_questions.a: Current is the same throughout — charge is not used up.

flashcard_questions.q: In a parallel circuit, how does potential difference compare across branches?
flashcard_questions.a: PD is the same across each branch, equal to the supply voltage.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to total resistance when you add a resistor in parallel?
flashcard_questions.a: Total resistance decreases — there are more paths for current to flow.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the voltage and frequency of the UK mains supply?

flashcard_questions.a: Current that constantly reverses direction, as produced by the mains supply.

flashcard_questions.q: Which wire must the fuse always be connected to, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: The live wire — so a fault breaks the live connection and makes the appliance safe.

flashcard_questions.q: State two power equations used in electrical circuits.

flashcard_questions.a: The energy transferred by a 1 kW device running for 1 hour.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the National Grid transmit electricity at high voltage?
flashcard_questions.a: High voltage means low current, reducing heat losses in cables (P = I²R).

flashcard_questions.q: Why do step-up and step-down transformers only work with AC?
flashcard_questions.a: They need a changing magnetic field to induce voltage — DC gives a constant field.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an RCD and how does it work?
flashcard_questions.a: A residual current device — detects a difference between live and neutral currents and cuts the circuit in milliseconds.

glossary_terms.definition: A circuit in which all components are connected in a single loop. Current is the same throughout; potential difference is shared between components.
A circuit in which components are connected on separate branches. Potential difference is the same across each branch; current is shared between branches.
Current that flows in one direction only, such as from a battery or solar cell.
Current that constantly reverses direction, alternating back and forth. UK mains supply is AC at 50 Hz and 230 V.
A safety device containing a thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit if the current exceeds a safe level. Always connected in the live wire.
A safety switch that detects tiny differences between the current in the live and neutral wires, cutting the circuit within milliseconds if current leaks.
The rate at which electrical energy is transferred in a circuit, measured in watts (W). 1 watt = 1 joule per second.
The UK's network of cables and transformers that distributes electricity from power stations to homes and businesses.
